extraction_text: Yudhishthira asks Vyasa about what actions require atonement and how to achieve liberation.

attributes.relationship: Grandson asks grandfather for spiritual guidance

extraction_text: Vyasa explains that people who do prohibited things or fail to do prescribed things should perform atonement.

Vyasa lists specific sins requiring atonement including sleeping at wrong times, improper marriage order, killing a Brahmin, slander, breaking vows, teaching Vedas to unworthy people, betraying the king, killing Sudra women, harming animals, defying teachers, abandoning sacred fire, and selling Vedic knowledge.

Vyasa lists additional prohibited actions including abandoning one's duty, performing others' duties, improper sacrifices, eating forbidden food, abandoning those seeking help, not supporting servants, selling intoxicants, cruelty to animals, not performing rituals when able, not giving charity, not paying fees, touching Brahmin property, sons separating from fathers, defiling teacher's bed, and illegitimate birth.

Vyasa explains exceptions where certain actions don't require atonement, including killing a Brahmin who attacks with weapons on battlefield, drinking intoxicants when near death, eating forbidden food if followed by purification, sleeping with teacher's wife for teacher's benefit, stealing for teacher's benefit in emergencies, stealing others' property (except Brahmin's) not for personal enjoyment, lying to save lives or for teacher/women/marriage, and nocturnal emissions in dreams.

attributes.action: Explaining circumstances where normally sinful actions don't require atonement

extraction_text: Vyasa cites the example of Uddalaka having his student father a son named Ketu (Comet) as precedent for sleeping with teacher's wife for teacher's benefit.
Vyasa explains methods for atonement and purification from sins.
Atonement through ascetic practices like begging, single daily meal, holding skull and staff, celibacy for twelve years removes sin of killing a Brahmin.
Six years of austerity or three years of monthly meals purifies killing a Brahmin sin.
Fasting quickly removes sins; performing sacrifices like Ashvamedha purifies.
Dying in battle for Brahmin's benefit removes sin of killing a Brahmin.
Donating 100,000 cows to worthy recipients removes all sins including Brahmin killing.
Smaller donations of cattle, horses, or discreet charity also remove sins.
Drinking hot liquids, jumping from mountains, entering fire, or long journeys purify Brahmin who drank alcohol.
Performing sacrifices according to Brihaspati's rules allows drinking Brahmin to rejoin community.
Abandoning envy, donating land, and abstaining from alcohol purifies drinker.
A person who defiles the teacher's bed should lie on a heated iron plate or wander as an ascetic holding his genitals, looking at the sky.

attributes.action: Prescribed penance for defiling teacher's bed

extraction_text: Evil karma can be removed by abandoning the body, by women through one year of effort, by performing great vows, giving away all property, or dying in battle for the teacher.
Telling lies to or disobeying the teacher can be atoned for by doing things that please the teacher.
Violating celibacy by ejaculation requires a vow like one who kills a Brahmin, wearing rough animal skin for six months.
Adultery with another's wife or stealing others' property requires observing a vow for one year.
Stealing property requires returning equivalent property to the owner.
Younger brother marrying before elder or elder marrying before younger requires strict vows for twelve nights for purification.
One can remarry to save ancestors; neither the man nor second wife incurs sin, nor is the first wife defiled.
Women are purified after four consecutive months of menstruation in cohabitation; purification occurs with menstruation onset.
Brahmins follow all dharma; Kshatriyas follow one-fourth less, Vaishyas one-fourth less than Kshatriyas, Shudras one-fourth less than Vaishyas.
Killing birds/animals or cutting many trees requires public confession, fasting three nights, and living on air.
Associating with forbidden persons requires penance: wearing wet clothes and lying on ash heap for six months.
All penance rules are established by Brahmins based on precedent, scriptures, and reasoning.
Reciting Savitri hymn in pure place, restrained diet, non-violence, non-stupidity, and non-garrulousness remove all sins.
Staying in open space day and night, entering water clothed for three days and nights.
Observing vows without speaking to women, Shudras, or outcastes removes unintentional sins for Brahmins.
After death, one receives good or bad results; the five elements are witnesses; good and bad karma cancel each other, leaving remaining results.
Good results increase through charity, austerity, and rituals; evil results increase through evil deeds.
With evil karma present, one should perform good deeds and frequently give charity to remove sin.
Penance methods are described; all except the most heinous sinners have redemption methods.
For eating forbidden food or speaking forbidden words, intentional acts are grave sins, unintentional are minor; both have penance methods.
King Yudhishthira (Dharmaraja) listens to the sage's words and reflects.

attributes.details: Should not give for fame, fear, or gratitude; prohibited recipients include actors, drunkards, madmen, outcastes, deformed persons, dwarves, wicked low-born people, and vow-breakers.

extraction_text: Warning about improper charity

attributes.details: Improper charity and acceptance are meaningless; compared to trying to swim ocean while holding heavy objects - both sink.

extraction_text: Criticism of unqualified Brahmins

attributes.details: Compared to wooden elephants, leather deer (empty names), eunuchs, barren cows, wingless birds; charity to them is like empty granary or dry well.

extraction_text: Qualification for receiving charity

attributes.details: May receive charity out of compassion if they lack Vedic knowledge but aren't hateful; wicked pitiable people should not receive charity.

attributes.details: Giving to Brahmins who abandon dharma is definitely wrong due to unworthiness of recipient.

extraction_text: Yudhishthira expresses his desire to learn about the duties of kings and all four castes in detail, and asks about strategies during crises and how to achieve victory while following dharma.

Yudhishthira mentions that previous discussions about expiation methods and permissible/impermissible foods have satisfied his curiosity, but he remains confused about the frequent conflict between fulfilling dharma and ruling a kingdom.
Sage Vyasa, a learned Vedic scholar who knows past and present, looks at Narada and advises Yudhishthira to go to Bhishma, the grandfather of the Kuru dynasty, to learn all about dharma.

Vyasa describes Bhishma's extensive knowledge and qualifications: born to the river goddess Ganga, he has seen gods led by Indra, pleased deities like Brihaspati with his conduct, learned statecraft, mastered scriptures known to Ushanas (teacher of gods and demons), studied Vedas from sages Vasistha and Bhrigu's descendant, learned from Sanatkumara (Brahma's eldest son), acquired ascetic practices from Markandeya, and obtained weapons from Rama and Indra.

Vyasa notes that although Bhishma is mortal, he controls his own death, and though childless, he enjoys a place in heaven. He is surrounded by holy sages and knows everything worth knowing, including the subtle meanings of dharma.

After hearing this, Yudhishthira, the far-sighted son of Kunti, tells Vyasa that he has committed horrifying slaughter of relatives, sinned against the whole world, become a destroyer of the earth, and used deceit to kill Bhishma who fought righteously, so he questions by what right he can now go to ask Bhishma.
